title: The Comment Said Otherwise: Reading Code You Did Not Write

questions.question: You are about to change a function whose comment says what it does. What is the right way to treat that comment?
options: As a specification you must not question
As a claim to be checked against the code, because nothing keeps the two in step
As noise, to be ignored and deleted
As a fact, since the author wrote it deliberately
questions.explanation: Measured on five functions: the comment was wrong in 12 of 25 cases, and exactly right for one of the five. Code changes more often than the comment above it.

questions.question: smooth is commented as an average with a factor of 0.2 that moves the estimate 20 percent towards each reading, and the code has alpha = 0.8 applied to the reading. What does smooth(10, 20) return?
options: 18, since the code moves 80 percent of the way
questions.explanation: estimate * (1 - 0.8) + reading * 0.8 = 2 + 16 = 18. The comment predicted 12. Five of the six cases disagreed, and tracing one by hand is how you find out.

questions.question: percent(raw) is raw * 100 / 1024 and its comment says 0 to 1023 maps to 0 to 100. What does percent(1023) return?
options: 99, because it divides by the number of values rather than the full scale and integer division truncates
questions.explanation: 1023 * 100 / 1024 is 99.9, truncated to 99. The full scale is 1023, one less than the number of values, so nothing ever reads 100.

questions.question: last_mean is commented 'mean of the last n readings, or of all of them if fewer', and it divides the sum by n. Given readings 2 and 4 with n of 4, what does it return?
options: 1.5, because the sum is 6 and it divides by 4
questions.explanation: The loop correctly sums only what exists; the divisor is the count asked for, not the count got. When there are n or more readings the two agree, which is why tests with plenty of data pass.

questions.question: Why does the suite include is_stale, whose comment is exactly right?
options: Because it has a bug the others lack
As a control: reading code is not distrusting it, it is finding out which comment is the wrong one
questions.explanation: 0 of 4 disagreed. A reader who distrusted everything would waste time on it, and one who trusted everything would be wrong about 12 cases in 25. The only way to tell is to trace.

questions.question: percent_exact divides by 1023 and nothing else. Why is rounding to the nearest percent left out of the fix?
options: It is a second, larger change: it moves 560 of 1024 answers, where dividing by 1023 moves 49, and it should be decided on its own
Rounding gives the wrong answer at 1023
Rounding is not possible with integers
questions.explanation: Change the least you can, and run the pin again. A fix that also changes what every caller has been getting makes it impossible to tell which change broke a result.
